title: Disaster rehearsal scenarios + terraform checklist for private deploys
content:
Purpose:
This draft is a working runbook for disaster rehearsal scenarios focused on private deployments (VPC + on-prem). It combines the operational playbook (what to do during an incident), a Terraform checklist for safe state and module upgrades, and a reproducible exercise plan to validate backups and restore procedures.

Scope:
- Applies to Private control plane + runtime clusters (on-prem and VPC-private) used by customers running Redwood Private.
- Covers core persistent components: etcd/control-plane state (k8s control plane where applicable), Redis/session caches, model artifact storage (object store or NFS), Postgres (metadata DB), Terraform remote state, and any S3-compatible backup targets (MinIO or S3).
- Excludes: hosted API, end-customer app data not managed by Redwood infra.

Goals of a rehearsal:
- Validate RTO/RPO assumptions for each component (targeted per-component SLAs below).
- Confirm Terraform state can be recovered and that module upgrades do not corrupt state.
- Exercise manual failover and automated fallback paths.
- Produce an actionable post-mortem & follow-up tasks.

Target RTO/RPO (current expectations)
- Object store (model artifacts): RTO 30m / RPO 1h (snapshot cadence dependent)
- Postgres metadata DB: RTO 15m / RPO 5m if WAL archiving configured; otherwise RTO 1h / RPO 1h
- etcd / k8s control-plane: RTO 5-15m (with healthy backups) / RPO 1-5m
- Redis (session/cache): RTO 5m / RPO best-effort (cache rebuild acceptable in many cases)
- Terraform remote state: RTO 10m / RPO none (state loss is catastrophic — avoid!)

Roles and communications
- Incident lead: Whoever is primary on-call for private-deployments (PagerDuty channel: #pdp-drill-ops)
- Terraform/infra lead: Priya Natarajan
- Database lead: Diego Alvarez
- Storage lead: Asha Rao
- Scribe: whoever is on-call not in hands-on
- Communications: eng-ops PM (announce to customer success if exercise impacts customers)

Pre-exercise checklist (48–72 hours prior)
- Create exercise ticket (Jira) and send calendar invite for all participants. Add a test customer tag.
- Snapshot Terraform remote state (terraform state pull > state-YYYYMMDD.json) and upload to private S3 path with versioning enabled.
- Ensure Velero backup schedule has at least one successful backup in last 24h (for k8s clusters).
- Verify Postgres base backups and WAL shipping are healthy; record last backup timestamp.
- Confirm Model artifact store has replication/versions enabled.
- Confirm S3/MinIO buckets have at-rest copies and lifecycle policy disabled for the exercise.
- Confirm access to recovery keys / KMS and that HSM creds are available.
- Validate that terraform modules intended for the exercise are on test branch (do NOT run against prod branch).

Exercise scenarios (pick 1–3 per run):
1) Full control-plane loss (simulate k8s master failure / etcd data corruption)
   - Detection: API server panics; control-plane nodes non-responsive; cluster health alerts fire.
   - Immediate action: Fail traffic to standby region if configured; set customer-facing feature flags to degraded.
   - Recovery path: restore etcd snapshot -> bring up control-plane -> validate worker nodes rejoin -> verify API responsiveness -> replay kube objects if needed (kubectl apply -f manifests-export.yaml).
   - Terraform notes: ensure cluster resources in state were not modified while control-plane was degraded; mark state as consistent by comparing state pull to expected.

2) Object-store corruption or accidental delete (model artifacts missing)
   - Detection: model pulls failing, 404s for artifacts, or integrity checks fail during startup.
   - Immediate action: switch runtime to read-only model cache if available; block writes to bucket to avoid further deletes.
   - Recovery path: restore latest snapshot to alternate bucket, run artifact integrity check script against restored bucket, update runtime config to point to restored bucket, run smoke test for model loads.
   - Terraform notes: if bucket resource was recreated, import into terraform state or run terraform state replace to avoid drift.

3) Postgres WAL gap or logical corruption
   - Detection: DB failing to accept writes or queries returning errors; monitoring alerts on replication lag.
   - Immediate action: promote standby replica if configured; pause write traffic; notify application owners.
   - Recovery path: apply WAL replay up to last consistent sequence; restore from base backup if WAL insufficient; run schema checks; run end-to-end regression tests for metadata APIs.

4) Terraform state loss/corruption (simulated by renaming remote state file)
   - Detection: terraform plan fails with inconsistent state or unknown resource IDs; CI runs break.
   - Immediate action: DO NOT run terraform apply to attempt to 'recreate' resources. Communicate to teams to pause infra changes.
   - Recovery path: retrieve last known-good state file from S3 versioning or state snapshot; run terraform state push with care using test workspace first; re-run terraform plan against a staging environment to validate.

Step-by-step recovery checklists (quick references)
- etcd restore (k8s clusters):
  1) Confirm etcd member endpoints and choose restore host (clean node).
  2) Stop kube-apiserver / controller-manager on hosts to avoid elections during restore.
  3) Use etcdctl snapshot restore: etcdctl snapshot restore snapshot.db --data-dir /var/lib/etcd-restored --name etcd-0 --initial-cluster ...
  4) Replace data-dir, start etcd, start control-plane, validate etcd health via etcdctl endpoint health.
  5) Validate API server; check pods and controllers.
  Pitfalls: wrong cluster-IDs in restored snapshot, mismatched member names. Keep a documented mapping of member names and IPs.

- Postgres restore (WAL + base backup):
  1) Take a copy of current data-dir (if present) to /tmp/pg-fallback-YYYYMMDD.
  2) Restore latest base backup to target data-dir.
  3) Ensure recovery.conf (or postgresql.auto.conf equivalent for our version) points to WAL archive location and correct restore_command.
  4) Start DB in recovery and monitor logs for completion.
  5) Run schema-housekeeping checks and run smoke queries (users count, recent job run checks).
  Pitfalls: mismatched Postgres major versions, missing extension files. Keep a matrix of supported DB versions per deployment.

- Object store (MinIO/S3) restore:
  1) Identify snapshot object prefix (s3://redwood-private/backups/<cluster>/models/YYYYMMDD/).
  2) Restore objects to a quarantine bucket first (to avoid overwriting).
  3) Run checksum verification (sha256) for a sample set of models.
  4) Update runtime config and switch traffic when verification is complete.

Terraform-specific checklist and notes
- Remote state: always use versioned S3-compatible backend with server-side encryption and DynamoDB or equivalent for state locking.
- State snapshotting: before any risky operation (module upgrade, provider upgrade, mass resource rename) run: terraform state pull > state-{{YYYYMMDD}}.json and push to backups bucket with immutability flag for at least 7 days.
- Workspaces: use per-environment workspaces (prod/stage/test) and never run prod apply from a non-prod workspace.
- Provider/module pinning: pin provider and module versions in root module to avoid accidental upgrades (example: terraform { required_providers { aws = { source = "hashicorp/aws" version = "~> 4.60" } } }).
- Provider upgrades: run terraform providers lock -platform=... and commit the .terraform.lock.hcl into repo. Test upgrades in a disposable environment.
- Safe plan/apply pattern (recommended):
  1) git branch per change; open PR; CI runs terraform fmt + validate + plan against a clone of remote state.
  2) Obtain approval; create a manual TODO in PR to snapshot state and create S3 backup.
  3) Run terraform apply in a single-user window with state locking verified (dynamodb or similar).
- State recovery commands (examples):
  - Pull state: terraform state pull > state-backup-20250301.json
  - Push state (dangerous): terraform state push state-backup-20250301.json  (ONLY after review and in maintenance window)
  - Replace provider when moving to new provider binary: terraform state replace-provider 'registry.terraform.io/old/provider' 'registry.terraform.io/new/provider'
  - Import resource into state: terraform import module.cluster.aws_instance.node i-0123456789abcdef0

Terraform module upgrade plan (mini playbook)
- Pre-upgrade: run module acceptance tests in an ephemeral account/cluster; check any module outputs that affect runtime (IPs, bucket names).
- During upgrade: (canary -> rollout) upgrade resources that are safe to replace first (stateless, external LB targets). Avoid mass replacements for stateful resources in same window.
- Post-upgrade validation: run an automated smoke test suite that covers API endpoints, model loads, and critical DB operations.
- Rollback: plan in advance how to reverse; often rollback means reverting module code and running terraform apply; but state-only rollbacks may be required (use state snapshots).

Automated backup tools and recommendations
- Velero: scheduled backups for k8s cluster namespaces that host runtime pods and CRDs. Store Velero snapshots in versioned S3 bucket.
- Object store: use native bucket versioning + lifecycle disabled for exercise; consider cross-region/object-replication for resilience.
- DB: pg_basebackup + WAL archiving to offsite bucket with daily retention. Test pg_basebackup restores quarterly.
- Terraform state: S3 + versioning + dedicated snapshot job that runs hourly for active projects.

Verification scripts (examples to keep in repo)
- verify-model-load.sh => pulls a sample model from object store and runs a tiny inference check
- smoke-postgres.sh => runs a set of queries (health counters) and verifies expected rows
- check-etcd-health.sh => runs etcdctl endpoint status against endpoints and validates member list matches expected inventory

Post-exercise capture and artefacts
- Collect: backup snapshots used, state-file copies, Velero logs, kube-apiserver logs around restore time, and timestamps for last successful backups.
- Post-mortem template items: what failed, time-to-detect, time-to-recover, steps that blocked recovery, missing scripts or perms, recommended follow-ups.
- Action items (example): tighten S3 bucket permissions, increase Velero retention for critical namespaces, add automated state snapshot pre-apply hook in CI.

Open questions / TODOs
- Decide retention policy for terraform state snapshots in customers' S3: 90 days vs 180 days? (Regulatory input needed.)
- Automate 'snapshot-and-lock' step in CI to create an immutable snapshot before major applies.
- Add simulated chaos test for partial network partition to measure degraded-path behavior.

Appendix: quick command references
- Snapshot state: terraform state pull > state-$(date +%Y%m%d).json
- Push state (emergency only): terraform state push state-YYYYMMDD.json
- List S3 object versions (awscli): aws s3api list-object-versions --bucket my-backups --prefix clusters/cluster-a/
- Run Velero restore: velero restore create --from-backup backup-20250228 --namespace redwood-runtime

Notes: This is intentionally a working draft. Expect iterations after the first 2 rehearsals. Please add detailed timestamps and 'what actually happened' sections to the Jira ticket after any run.
